analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder to sue companies over Year 2000 computer failures by adding notice rules and damage limits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 1999 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for lawsuits arising from the Year 2000 (Y2K) computer-date problem. Before suing, a plaintiff would have to give 90 days' written notice and plead damages in exact detail. It would make every written contract term — including liability caps and warranty disclaimers — fully enforceable, limit each defendant to paying only its own share of fault, bar most lawsuits for purely financial losses, and let courts throw out class actions unless a majority of the class suffered a major defect. Personal-injury claims and government enforcement actions were carved out.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be companies that sold or built computers, software, and equipment with embedded chips — the defendants in any wave of Y2K lawsuits — along with their insurers. Contract liability caps and warranty disclaimers would become fully enforceable, a 'reasonable efforts' defense would let companies escape paying for failures they tried in good faith to fix, and each defendant would pay only its own percentage of fault rather than the whole judgment. Businesses that feared being dragged into litigation would also gain.

how_it_helps.text: Requires plaintiffs to give defendants 90 days' written notice before filing a Y2K lawsuit, and lets a defendant immediately sue-blocking procedures if the notice rules weren't followed, giving companies a delay and a settlement window before any case starts.

Makes all written contract terms, including limits or exclusions of liability and warranty disclaimers, fully enforceable in Y2K claims, so companies that contracted around Y2K responsibility could not be sued around those caps.
Creates a complete defense for defendants who took 'reasonable measures' to prevent a Y2K failure, and gives them a 'reasonable efforts' evidence option to reduce damages in contract breach claims.

Limits each defendant to paying only its own percentage share of a judgment (with carve-outs for low-net-worth individuals and knowing misconduct), bars most tort recovery for purely economic losses like lost profits, and requires a court to find a 'material defect' affecting a majority of a class before a Y2K class action can proceed.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on anyone harmed by a Y2K failure who would have to sue — particularly consumers and small businesses that lost money, data, or working equipment. They would face a mandatory 90-day delay, detailed pleading requirements that could get their case dismissed, strict limits on recovering purely financial losses, unenforceable-in-practice contract caps honored against them, and a much harder path to bringing a class action.
analysis.who_pays_short: People and small businesses hurt by Y2K failures

drawbacks.text: The bill would make boilerplate contract terms — liability caps and warranty disclaimers — fully enforceable against buyers in Y2K disputes, overriding contrary state law, so a company that sold a defective product could escape paying for the damage its own contract paperwork disclaimed.

It would bar recovery of economic losses (lost profits, business interruption, lost data) in tort except in narrow circumstances, leaving many plaintiffs with real financial losses from a defective product no way to recover at all.

A class action over a defective product could proceed only if the court found the defect was 'material' for a majority of class members, which would let companies facing widespread but individually small failures avoid group lawsuits entirely.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: small businesses and individuals with genuine Y2K losses would face real hurdles to being made whole, though the bill did preserve personal-injury claims, government enforcement actions, and a joint-liability backstop for plaintiffs worth under $200,000 whose damages exceeded 10% of their net worth.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the companies it aimed to protect, the bill was thoughtfully designed: it targeted frivolous suits, encouraged settlement, and kept the courts open for real injury — including personal injury and a carve-out for low-net-worth plaintiffs. But the price of that protection fell on the other side of the same transactions: people and small businesses harmed by defective products would have found it substantially harder to recover their financial losses, because contract disclaimers became airtight, economic-loss suits were largely barred, and class actions were gated behind a 'majority of the class' test. The bill weighted the scales toward defendants far more than existing law did.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Dodd introduced the Y2K Fairness in Litigation Act on March 25, 1999, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The bill never received any further action — no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote — and it died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

The issue it addressed did not disappear: Congress passed and the President signed a separate, broader Y2K liability law in July 1999 that included many of the same defendant protections — notice-and-waiting periods, pleading requirements, proportionate liability, and limits on punitive damages — so that law, not this bill, governed actual Y2K lawsuits.

The bill's stated aim was to keep producers and users of technology focused on fixing the Y2K problem rather than fighting lawsuits, and to discourage 'insubstantial' litigation while preserving complete relief for real injury.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies facing potential Y2K lawsuits came out ahead: they got most of the protections this bill sought through the separate Y2K Act signed into law in July 1999, while ordinary plaintiffs were left with the weakened recourse that law created rather than the even-tighter rules this bill would have added.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held: a Democratic senator sponsored the bill with two Democratic cosponsors, and it died without recorded opposition in the Republican-led Judiciary Committee.

industries.note: The bill would have made their liability caps and warranty disclaimers fully enforceable, added a 90-day notice delay before suits, created a 'reasonable efforts' defense, and limited their share of any judgment to their percentage of fault — directly reducing what buyers could recover for defective products.

Y2K claims covered any device with an embedded microchip, so makers of everything from medical devices to industrial controls would have gained the same shields against suits over products that failed on the date change.
Fewer, narrower Y2K lawsuits and smaller judgments mean fewer liability payouts; the industry's gain comes out of plaintiffs' recovery.

The bill's pleading requirements, class-action thresholds, and economic-loss bar would shrink the pool of viable Y2K cases that lawyers could take on contingency, and their interest here runs with their clients' ability to recover.
